newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Landsbergis seals comeback with poll landslide.
newsitem.headline: Landsbergis seals comeback with poll landslide.

text.p: The leader of Lithuania's struggle to quit the former Soviet Union, Vytautas Landsbergis, completed his political comeback on Monday when his party emerged the landslide winner of a second round of elections.
With most votes counted in the 65 seats under contention, Landsbergis' right-wing Homeland Union party had won 35 of them, preliminary final figures showed.
His party fell just one seat short of a majority in the Baltic state's 141-seat parliament, having also won 35 seats in the first round on October 20.

But the Homeland Union had already pledged to form a coalition with the Christian Democratic party, which got four seats in the second round to add to its 11 in the first. The coalition will thus have a healthy majority.

As in the first round, Sunday's poll was marked by a large degree of voter apathy. Just 36.53 percent of the electorate had voted two hours before the polls closed, compared with 48.08 percent at the same stage in the first round.
The results marked a remarkable comeback by Landsbergis, who was humiliated at the ballot box in 1992 by his enemies, the reformed communists of the Lithuanian Democratic Labour Party (LDLP).
The LDLP won only 10 seats in the first round of the latest elections and just two in the second, the preliminary figures showed.
Landsbergis, a short and stocky former music professor, spearheaded Lithuania's drive for independence from the former Soviet Union in a head-on confrontation with Moscow.

He refused to back down even after 13 people were killed in a Soviet army assault on Vilnius television tower in January 1991, one of the bloodiest incidents to accompany the collapse of Soviet power.

But with his Sajudis independence movement riven by internal fighting and the economy collapsing after the break with Moscow, Landsbergis was rejected in the 1992 elections in favour of the LDLP, formed from the old Lithuanian Communist Party.

The LDLP sealed its victory in 1993 when its leader, Algirdas Brazauskas, was elected president. It also started a trend in eastern Europe, where ex-communists were often propelled back to power by people wearied by economic hardship.

The Homeland Union-dominated government is expected to keep Lithuania on the path to European Union and NATO membership but some aspects of its economic policy, such as the unpegging of its currency from the dollar, have worried foreign investors.
Landsbergis is now expected to become speaker of the new parliament, a position which commentators say will enable him to prepare for a 1998 presidential battle against Brazauskas.
The new prime minister will be Gediminas Vagnorius, who held the post in 1991-92 and is now one of the Homeland Union's main leaders.

Western diplomats say Landsbergis will need to learn to tone down his confrontational rhetoric, which has been directed at the West for being too slow to accept Lithuania into its security structures as often as against Russia, his traditional opponent.
